Severity should be MEDIUM, not high. The finding bundles a low-impact PRESENT bug (over-count = 1 wasted RTT, and the read-after-move is currently harmless because the move is a shallow copy) with a hypothetical FUTURE high-impact bug (if someone implements a real move, Slices silently becomes 1 → truncated/corrupt transfer). The dramatic "stuck on loading → 10s timeout → entry removed → next ack null-derefs → crash" causal chain is not produced by the over-count; the over-count completes normally with a wasted round-trip. The null-deref crash and the truncation are real but independent of the over-count. Correct severity for the present state is low-to-medium; the latent-trap (correct move breaks Slices) and the unchecked Find null-deref are the genuinely concerning parts and justify medium.</corrections>
<parameter name="extraInsight">Additional independent defect the finding missed, which strengthens the "fragile completion" concern: `Slices` is declared `int64_t` (RCO.h:16) but is passed as the 3rd argument to `ClientReceiveInitialBuildingData(SendBuffer, Size, Slices)` (RCO.cpp:79), whose parameter is `int16 TotalSliceCount` (RCO.h:76), and `ReceivedSliceCount` is also `int16` (RCO.h:91). For any factory whose serialized size exceeds 32767*2047 ≈ 67 MB, Slices truncates/wraps to int16 and the equality check `ReceivedSliceCount == TotalSliceCount` (line 103) can never match correctly → permanent stuck transfer → the real 10s timeout (line 90) → entry removed → a late ack then null-derefs at line 73 (`*Find(...)`). That is the actual, code-supported path to issue #9 (dedicated-server join crash) and #14, and it does not depend on the move bug at all. Also note `Size` is `int16` (line 77) but BuildingDataBufferMaxSize=2047 fits fine; the int16 risk is specifically on the slice COUNT, not the per-slice size.

Two small precision notes, neither weakens the high severity: (1) The 'NaN progress' claim is imprecise — a negative wrapped TotalSliceCount gives a NEGATIVE (bogus) progress value, not NaN; true NaN/inf (divide-by-zero) only occurs in the narrow case where the slice count wraps to exactly 0 (an exact multiple of 65536 slices ~= 134MB, 268MB, ...). 'Bogus progress bar' is the accurate framing. (2) The per-building byte estimate is correct in spirit but worth pinning: it depends on FBufferWriter NOT being a bit-packed net archive — I verified ArIsNetArchive is explicitly disabled (cpp:46), so SerializeBits rounds each field up to whole bytes; if a future change re-enabled net-archive bit packing, the byte rate (and thus the building-count threshold, not the 67MB threshold) would shift. The 67MB / ~32767-slice overflow threshold itself is independent of the per-building rate and is exact.
verdicts.extraInsight: Related defect in the SAME overflow neighborhood, worth a separate finding: even before the int16 overflow, FBuildingDataBuffer (RCO.h:36-44) is a USTRUCT containing a fixed `uint8 Data[2047]` array that is replicated by value, and FBuildingDataBuffer::NetSerialize (RCO.cpp:15-20) ALWAYS serializes the full BuildingDataBufferMaxSize (2047 bytes) regardless of the actual `Size` — the last/partial slice still pushes a full 2047-byte struct over the wire and memcpys garbage tail bytes into SendBuffer (cpp:76-78 only copies `Size` valid bytes, leaving Data[Size..2047) uninitialized stack memory that is then transmitted). That is both a minor bandwidth waste and a potential info-leak of uninitialized server stack memory to clients. Separately, the whole transfer holds the ENTIRE serialized CurrentBuildingData (tens of MB) resident on BOTH server (FBufferWriter, freed only on Finished/timeout, RCO.cpp:67/88) and client (TArray<uint8> Buffer accumulates every slice, RCO.cpp:97, never reserved/freed until deserialize) — this compounds the mod's known high-memory complaint during joins. Also: the server's per-slice timer is reset to 10s on every slice send (cpp:83), so a healthy transfer is fine, but there is no cap on total transfer time and no backpressure, matching the author's own admitted limitation (cpp:11-13).

verdicts.corrections:
Byte estimate overstated. The "~67MB-class per copy / tens of MB" figure assumes serialized size tracks in-memory sizeof(FBuildingData) (~150-200B with FTransform + two std::variants + caches). It does NOT: FBuildingData::NetSerialize (CartographDataStructure.cpp:118-206) is a quantized serializer — hash 4B (SerializeBits 32), packed location ~13B (SerializePackedVector<1,24>), compressed rotation ~6B (SerializeCompressedShort), 2-bit extra-data index ~1B; caches (DataCache/LayerDataCache/VisualBoxCache) are never serialized. Net: a normal icon/rectangle building ≈ 24-28 bytes, a spline (belt/pipe, 9 quantized points via SPLINE_SEGMENTS+1) ≈ ~100 bytes, on this archive. Realistic per-copy buffer: ~3-15 MB for a typical large factory (100k-300k buildables); ~30-60 MB only at the extreme spline-heavy ≥1M-buildable end — so "tens of MB" is defensible only at the very top of the range, not the norm. Keep severity HIGH (the game-thread hitch + per-concurrent-transfer multiplication is the real cost; even a 5-10 MB synchronous serialize + realloc-copy burst on the sim tick is a multi-frame stall), but the memory/byte numbers should be cut ~3-5x for typical saves.</corrections>
<parameter name="extraInsight">Two related issues found. (a) The serializer is unintentionally ~2-4x larger than intended on the wire AND in this buffer: ArIsNetArchive is explicitly NOT set (RCO.cpp:46 commented out), so the FBufferWriter is a plain BYTE archive — every SerializeBits/SerializeInt call in NetSerialize and WriteQuantizedVector2D rounds up to whole bytes instead of true bit-packing. So all the bit-level quantization effort is wasted on the server-side buffer; switching to a bit writer (or just sending raw and relying on per-slice replication) would shrink the buffer 2-4x and proportionally cut the alloc/hitch. (b) Latent bug at RCO.cpp:52-53: `std::move(Archive)` into the struct member, then `Archive.TotalSize()` is read on the moved-from object on line 53 to compute Slices. The comment at line 40 ("FBufferWriter doesn't handle moving properly") confirms there's no real move ctor, so it currently happens to work (shallow copy leaves Archive's size intact), but it is fragile — if FBufferWriter ever gains a proper move ctor that nulls the source, Slices becomes 1 and the transfer silently breaks. The fix path for the finding (serialize off-thread / incrementally, or maintain a single shared serialized snapshot reused across all pending transfers instead of one copy per player) also resolves the unshared-memory multiplication.

findings.title: BuildingDataIndexRedirector forces a full O(N) array scan on EVERY single add/remove (the core lag-spike multiplier)
findings.mechanism: The triad is held together by BuildingDataIndexRedirector, a parallel array bridging quadtree element-ids -> indices into the Z-sorted CurrentBuildingData. Because CurrentBuildingData is kept sorted by Z and insertion shifts all later indices, every mutation must re-base the redirector. OnBuildingDataAdd (cpp:1199-1206) loops over the ENTIRE redirector and increments every entry >= Pos, then appends; OnBuildingDataRemove (cpp:1217-1230) loops the ENTIRE redirector to find the matching slot, calls QuadTree.Remove, sets that slot to -1, and decrements every entry > Pos. Both are O(N) per single building, where N = total buildings in the save. RedrawMapCoroutine calls these inside the per-building loop (cpp:574, 596), and CurrentBuildingData.Insert/RemoveAt (cpp:575, 597) are themselves O(N) memmoves. So placing/removing K buildings in one batch costs O(K*N). For a mid-to-large factory (N=100k-500k) every belt/pole placement triggers a 100k-500k-element scan PLUS a 100k-500k-element memmove of FBuildingData (~150-200 bytes each) — tens of ms to multiple seconds, exactly matching issue #14's 'up to 15s' spikes after 1.2 (1.2 introduced lightweight buildables that arrive in huge replicated/save batches, so K is large too). The redirector ALSO never shrinks: removed entries become -1 tombstones (h:363 comment confirms it is never .Remove()'d), so the scan length and the redirector's memory grow monotonically with lifetime build+remove churn and never recover, feeding the well-known high-memory complaint.
findings.fixDirection: Decouple identity from array position: give each building a stable id via TSparseArray<FBuildingData> with generation handles (or a TMap<Id,FBuildingData>); store that stable id in the quadtree so adds/removes never re-base anything. Delete BuildingDataIndexRedirector entirely. This turns add/remove from O(N) into O(log N) (quadtree) + O(1) (sparse-array slot reuse), eliminating both the per-event scan and the tombstone leak.

findings.title: Sorting the master array by Z couples the height-filter to storage and is the only reason positions are unstable
findings.mechanism: CurrentBuildingData is kept globally sorted by Z purely so the Z-height filter can range-select with Algo::LowerBound(MinZFilter)/UpperBound(MaxZFilter) (cpp:663-664; operator<=> compares only Transform.Z, DataStructure.cpp:23-32). That single design choice is what makes array positions unstable on insert, which in turn necessitates the redirector and its O(N) fixups (finding redirector-on-mutation). The Z-filter itself is used rarely (only when the user drags the height slider, OnZFilterUpdated cpp:935), yet it taxes EVERY build event. Worse, in the partial-redraw path the code pays for BOTH structures redundantly: it queries the quadtree by area (cpp:686), maps every result through the redirector (cpp:689-692), Algo::Sort's the indices (cpp:693), then does FindByPredicate/FindLastByPredicate to intersect with the Z-range (cpp:696-708) — an O(M log M) sort of the candidate set on every partial redraw just to reconcile spatial results back into Z-order. The spatial query and the Z-filter are logically independent but are forced through one ordered array.
findings.fixDirection: Decouple Z from spatial storage: keep buildings in a stable-id store (unordered) and maintain a SEPARATE Z-index — either a sorted TArray<TPair<float,Id>> (or TSet) updated O(log N) per mutation, or coarse Z-band buckets (e.g. 1m bands -> TMap<int32,TArray<Id>>). Store a per-building Z (or band) alongside the quadtree element so the area query can filter by Z inline without a global sort. The master store then needs no ordering and positions stay stable.

findings.title: Maintaining a full second copy of every buildable (FBuildingData ~150-200B x N) is the dominant memory cost and is largely redundant with the game's own subsystems
findings.mechanism: CurrentBuildingData stores one heavyweight FBuildingData per buildable forever. Each element holds an FTransform (~64B: quat+translation+scale), TWO std::variants — BuildableExtraData (monostate/FSplineExtraData{TArray<FVector2D>}/FWireExtraData/FBeamExtraData) and DataCache (FNormalDataCache{FVector2D+FVector2D+FRotator+variant<TSoftObjectPtr,FRectangleDataCache{ptr+4xFVector=~104B}>}) — plus FBox2D VisualBoxCache, a layer-data pointer, an enum and a hash (DataStructure.h:76-109). Conservatively 150-200 bytes/building, much of it (ScreenPosition, Corners, Size, Rotation) DERIVED data that could be recomputed at draw time. At N=200k that is ~30-40 MB just for the array, plus the quadtree's per-node element arrays, plus the never-shrinking redirector (4B*N + tombstones), plus a spline's TArray<FVector2D>(9 pts) heap allocation per spline buildable. On the host this fully duplicates AFGBuildableSubsystem::GetAllBuildablesRef and AFGLightweightBuildableSubsystem::mBuildableClassToInstanceArray (the very sources gathered at init, cpp:383-388) — the host could query those on-demand per redraw region and keep only lightweight render metadata + a spatial index. On dedicated-server CLIENTS those subsystems lack the data (hence the RCO transfer), so clients must keep some store — but it can be the slim render-metadata form, not the full FBuildingData with all caches.
findings.fixDirection: Split storage into a tiny persistent record {classHash, transform (or quantized pos+rot), Z, extraData-for-splines/wires} and recompute all draw-time caches (screen pos, corners, tile size) lazily during the draw loop. On the host, prefer iterating AFGBuildableSubsystem/AFGLightweightBuildableSubsystem for the dirty region instead of holding a parallel array; keep only the spatial index + Z-index of stable ids. Keep the slim record only on clients that received it via RCO. This roughly halves-to-quarters per-building bytes and removes derived-data duplication.

findings.title: A persistent quadtree keyed by unstable ids is the wrong index for a write-heavy, fixed-bounds, redraw-by-radius workload; a uniform hash grid fits better
findings.mechanism: The world bounds are fixed and known at compile time (WEST/EAST/NORTH/SOUTH_BOUND, h:28-31; ~7500m x 7500m). The dominant operations are (a) point/box insert on every build event and (b) box query over the small redraw area (RedrawArea = union of changed buildings' VisualBoxCache, expanded by 300cm, DataStructure.cpp:482/545). TQuadTree allocates/splits nodes and stores ElementType in per-node arrays; with the current scheme each Remove must be matched by re-finding the element-id, and the tree is rebuilt wholesale on Empty() at every InitialBuildableGather (cpp:469). For a uniform, dense, fixed-extent factory map this is more overhead and worse cache behavior than a flat uniform hash grid: cells sized to the typical redraw radius (a building's clearance box + 300cm, i.e. a few meters to a few tens of meters) give O(1) insert, O(1) remove (store stable id in a TSet/TArray per cell), and a box query that visits only the handful of overlapping cells. It also sidesteps the quadtree's id-stability problem because grid cells hold stable ids directly. Memory is bounded and predictable (grid dimensions fixed), avoiding pointer-chasing node allocations.
findings.fixDirection: Replace TQuadTree<int32> with a uniform hash grid TMap<FIntPoint,TArray<BuildingId>> (or a flat 2D array of cells, since bounds are fixed) with cell size tuned to the typical building+expansion footprint. Insert/remove a stable id into the cell(s) the VisualBox overlaps; box query iterates overlapping cells only. O(1) mutation, no node splitting, cache-friendly, bounded memory. Keep the quadtree only if buildings were sparse — they are not.

findings.title: Redraw scope is a single union AABB, not per-tile dirty regions, so multi-region edits clear+redraw a giant bounding rectangle (overdraw at 8192x8192)
findings.mechanism: Partial redraw accumulates ONE FBox2D RedrawArea = union of all changed buildings' VisualBoxCache for the whole batch (cpp:570, 593), converts it to one ScissorArea (cpp:639-645), then clears and redraws everything intersecting that single rectangle. If a batch touches two far-apart areas (common: paste a blueprint here, dismantle there; or a long belt run), the union rectangle spans the gap and the scissor covers a huge region of the 8192x8192 (RENDER_TEXTURE_SIZE, h:35) target, so the full-screen ClearItem (cpp:653-660) plus all buildings inside that span are re-rasterized — large GPU fill cost. This compounds with the CPU O(K*N) cost above and plausibly contributes to issue #14's GPU TDR (driver timeout) over a long session: repeated large clears+draws on an 8192^2 RT under accumulating CPU stalls. There is also no per-tile invalidation, so the renderer cannot skip untouched tiles or coalesce/throttle redraws by tile.
findings.fixDirection: Partition the render target into fixed tiles (e.g. 256x256 or 512x512 px). On mutation, mark only the tiles overlapping each changed VisualBox dirty (a TSet<FIntPoint>); per frame, process a budgeted number of dirty tiles, clearing+redrawing each tile's scissor rect independently using the hash-grid query for that tile. This bounds clear+overdraw to actually-changed tiles, enables a frame-relative redraw budget (issue #10's request), and naturally supports an explicit user-triggered full redraw by marking all tiles dirty.

findings.title: Z-filter change and layer-config change force a full entire redraw, re-walking and re-rasterizing all N buildings
findings.mechanism: OnZFilterUpdated (cpp:935-950) and OnLayerConfigChanged (cpp:407-413) both call RedrawMap(true) -> bRedrawEntirely. The entire path builds BuildingsToDraw = [Min,Max) over the WHOLE Z-range slice of CurrentBuildingData (cpp:676-683) and redraws every one with a full 8192^2 clear. With the current single sorted array this is the only option, but it means a trivial UI interaction (nudging the height slider, toggling a layer) is an O(N) CPU walk + full-RT rasterization — on a large base this is itself a multi-hundred-ms-to-second hitch and interacts badly with the coroutine-cancel/restart logic (RedrawMap cancels an in-flight coroutine and re-queues, cpp:437-450), so rapid slider drags can thrash full redraws. A decoupled Z-index + tile system would let a Z-filter change re-evaluate only tiles whose contents cross the new threshold, and a layer toggle only tiles containing that layer.
findings.fixDirection: With the Z-index + tile architecture, treat filter/layer changes as 'invalidate tiles affected by the predicate change' rather than a global redraw; debounce slider input (coalesce to one redraw per N ms). Reserve true full redraw for an explicit user button (per issue #10).

findings.title: Recommended end-state architecture and migration path
findings.mechanism: Target data model (decoupled triad): (1) STORE = TSparseArray<FSlimBuildingRecord> with generation handles; FSlimBuildingRecord = {uint32 classHash, FTransform transform (or quantized pos+rot), float z, slim extra-data for spline/wire/beam}. All draw-time caches (screen pos, corners, tile size, category/layer ptr) computed lazily in the draw loop, not stored. Stable BuildingId = sparse-array handle; never remaps on insert/remove. (2) SPATIAL = uniform hash grid TMap<FIntPoint,TArray<BuildingId>> over the fixed world bounds, cell ~= typical building+300cm footprint; O(1) insert/remove of stable ids, region query visits overlapping cells. (3) Z-INDEX = separate sorted structure (sorted TArray<TPair<float,BuildingId>> or Z-band buckets) for the height filter, updated O(log N) per mutation. (4) RENDER = fixed tile grid over the 8192^2 RT with a dirty-tile set and a per-frame tile budget; mutation marks overlapping tiles dirty; full redraw = mark all dirty. This makes per-event cost O(log N) insert + O(1) grid + mark-dirty, with zero global array fixups and no tombstone leak, directly resolving #14's spikes and #10's localized/budgeted redraw request, and cutting memory by storing slim records + bounded grid/tile structures instead of full FBuildingData + ever-growing redirector. On the HOST, optionally drop the STORE entirely and iterate AFGBuildable/Lightweight subsystems per dirty tile (they already hold the data); keep STORE only on dedicated-server clients fed by the existing RCO transfer.
findings.fixDirection: Migration: Step 1 (highest ROI, low risk) — replace BuildingDataIndexRedirector + sorted-array-position ids with a TSparseArray stable-id store; quadtree stores stable ids; OnBuildingDataAdd/Remove become O(1)/O(log N). This alone kills the #14 spike and the redirector memory leak while keeping the existing quadtree and Z-array-as-index. Step 2 — extract a standalone Z-index so the master store no longer needs Z-sorting. Step 3 — swap quadtree for a uniform hash grid. Step 4 — add tile-based dirty rendering with a per-frame budget + explicit full-redraw button. Steps are independently shippable and each reduces cost.

verdicts.corrections: Severity critical is appropriate. Two estimate corrections, both making the finding WORSE not better: (a) The per-element byte estimate of "150-200 bytes" is understated. FBuildingData (CartographDataStructure.h:75-109) = uint32(4) + FTransform (UE5 double-precision: quat 32 + translation 24 + scale 24 = ~80) + std::variant BuildableExtraData(~32) + enum(4) + std::variant DataCache whose largest alternative FNormalDataCache is ~80 (two FVector2D=32, FRotator=24, inner variant ~24) + LayerDataCache ptr(8) + FBox2D(~40), realistically ~250-320 bytes/element. So the CurrentBuildingData.Insert/RemoveAt memmove moves more bytes than claimed. (b) The redirector scan length is NOT N=live buildings but (live + accumulated tombstones), i.e. the count of valid-box buildings ever added over the session. So OnBuildingDataAdd/Remove's O(N) scan is strictly larger than the live-count N and grows even when the live factory size is stable -- the scan does not recover when buildings are removed, only the memmove length tracks live count. The redirector scan is over int32 (4 bytes), so the memmove on CurrentBuildingData is the dominant constant; the two O(N) passes are additive.
verdicts.extraInsight: Two adjacent problems worth flagging. (1) Same-Z worst case: because the sort key is only Z (DataStructure.cpp:23-26), the very common case of many buildables at the same ground Z (foundations, belts, poles) makes Algo::LowerBound land at the START of the equal-Z run, maximizing both the memmove distance in CurrentBuildingData and the number of redirector entries with Index>=Pos that must be incremented -- so the realistic constant factor on big flat factories is near worst-case, not average. (2) The remove path has a SECOND O(N) scan beyond the redirector: cpp:584-605 linearly scans CurrentBuildingData from the LowerBound position forward comparing with operator== (which does FTransform.Equals + BuildableExtraData compare) to find the exact element among same-Z duplicates, before calling OnBuildingDataRemove. So a single remove is effectively O(N) scan of CurrentBuildingData (cpp:587) + O(N) redirector scan (cpp:1218) + O(N) memmove (cpp:597) = three O(N) operations. The algorithmic fix is to replace the parallel-array+tombstone+sorted-vector design with a stable handle map (quadtree element-id -> a slot in a free-list-backed pool, with draw order maintained separately, e.g. a per-Z bucket or an order index sorted lazily only at redraw), which turns add/remove into O(log N) (quadtree) + O(1) (pool slot) instead of 3x O(N).

verdicts.corrections: Severity high is appropriate; the per-build tax is genuine. Two precision corrections: (a) The per-event cost that "taxes every build" is the O(N) redirector fixup + mid-array Insert/RemoveAt shift (cpp:575,597,1199-1230), not the LowerBound/UpperBound Z queries (those are only O(log N) and run once per redraw, cpp:663-664). The analyst's headline framing ("the Z-filter... taxes EVERY build event") is right about the symptom but the mechanism is the sorted *storage*, not the filter query. (b) The Algo::Sort at cpp:693 is not strictly required even for the current Z-trim: the [Min,Max) intersection could be done with a per-element predicate test (Min<=idx<Max) without sorting, since draw order is irrelevant. So the O(M log M) sort is gratuitous and removable independently — strengthening, not weakening, the "needless coupling" claim.
verdicts.extraInsight: The redirector is append-only: OnBuildingDataRemove (cpp:1217-1230) tombstones the removed slot to -1 rather than removing it, and the comment at h:363 confirms it "doesn't get .Remove()'d". Combined with the O(N) full-array scan on EVERY add and remove (cpp:1199, 1218), this makes both build and remove O(N) in the cumulative number of buildings ever placed, not the live count — a monotonically growing cost that directly explains GitHub #14's lag spikes scaling with factory age. A spatially-keyed structure that stored stable element ids (e.g. a free-list / generational handle, or storing CurrentBuildingData in stable slots and keeping a separate Z-sorted index array) would decouple the Z-filter from storage and eliminate both the O(N) redirector fixup and the partial-path Sort. Also worth flagging: the remove loop at cpp:587-605 does a linear scan from LowerBound forward through all equal-Z entries to find the exact match via operator==, so dense same-Z factories (e.g. a flat floor of foundations all at one Z) degrade removal toward O(N) on top of the redirector cost.

verdicts.corrections:
Two quantitative corrections, both making the problem WORSE, not better:

1) Per-element byte size is understated. With UE5's default double-precision math types, sizeof(FBuildingData) is ~344B (I compiled a faithful mock: FTransform=80, FNormalDataCache=168, DataCache variant=176, FBox2D=40), not 150-200B. The 150-200B figure would only hold if the build used the legacy single-precision (LWC-off) FVector, which Satisfactory/UE5.3 does not. Therefore at N=200k the array is ~69 MB, not "30-40 MB". The analyst's range is a safe floor but ~2x low.

2) The TSoftObjectPtr variant member is heavier than implied but irrelevant to the max: std::variant<TSoftObjectPtr<UTexture2D>, FRectangleDataCache> is sized by the larger arm (FRectangleDataCache=104B), so TSoftObjectPtr's exact size doesn't change the per-element total. No impact on the conclusion.

Severity "high" is appropriate and arguably understated given the ~2x larger real per-element size. Keep at high.
verdicts.extraInsight: Related amplifier I noticed while verifying: the duplication is not just a steady-state RAM cost — it is also re-paid as transient churn. (a) OnBuildingDataAdd (cpp:1199-1205) does an O(N) linear scan over the entire BuildingDataIndexRedirector to increment indices on EVERY single add, and OnBuildingDataRemove (cpp:1217-1230) does the same O(N) scan on every remove. Combined with the never-shrinking tombstoned redirector, a session that builds and demolishes a lot makes both the array AND these per-event scans grow, so the memory bloat directly feeds the O(N)-per-event CPU cost behind issue #14's lag spikes. (b) FSplineExtraData.Points.Reserve(SPLINE_SEGMENTS=8) at cpp:225 under-reserves for the 9 points actually added at cpp:227 (loop runs SPLINE_SEGMENTS+1 times), forcing a TArray growth realloc on every spline — a small but pure-waste per-spline allocation. (c) Splines pay double: they store the 9-point FSplineExtraData heap array AND keep it for the whole session even though the VisualBox and draw could be regenerated. Slimming the element and dropping the derived caches would shrink RAM and remove the realloc, addressing both the memory complaint and part of #14 at once.

verdicts.corrections: Memory estimate is understated/misattributed in one respect: the dominant memory consumer is the 8192x8192 render target itself (RENDER_TEXTURE_SIZE=8192, Public/CartographGameInstanceModule.h:35; the RT is a UCanvasRenderTarget2D, h:335, driven entirely against RENDER_TEXTURE_SIZE, e.g. ScissorArea/transforms cpp:635, 639-645). At RGBA8 that is 8192^2 x 4 = 268 MB; at the higher-precision formats canvas RTs commonly use (RGBA16f) it is ~537 MB, and with mips/double-buffering close to 1 GB. The proposed slim-record + bounded-grid changes attack the per-building heap (~150-200B/record) and the redirector leak, but do NOT touch the RT, which dominates the well-known "high memory" complaint. The finding should explicitly list the render-target resolution/format (e.g. tiled or lower-res RT, single-channel/indexed format) as a separate, larger memory lever orthogonal to the STORE redesign; otherwise the "cutting memory by storing slim records instead of full FBuildingData" line overstates how much of the headline memory the data-model change recovers.
verdicts.extraInsight: Two related problems reinforcing this finding: (1) The remove path in RedrawMapCoroutine is itself O(N) beyond the redirector: for each removed building it does Algo::LowerBound then a linear forward scan from Start to find the exact match (cpp:584-599) before the O(N) RemoveAt — so a batch of K removals is O(K*N). The stable-id grid model makes removal a direct O(1) sparse-array free + grid-cell erase, removing this scan entirely. (2) The redirector tombstone leak has a correctness hazard, not just a memory one: GetElements returns redirector indices that may now point at tombstoned (-1) slots; cpp:691 dereferences BuildingDataIndexRedirector[Index] unconditionally, so a -1 can flow into BuildingsToDraw and then index CurrentBuildingData[i] at cpp:717 (CurrentBuildingData[-1]) unless filtered by the later Z-range predicates — the Algo::Sort at cpp:693 pushes -1 entries to the front and the FindByPredicate Min cutoff (cpp:696) usually trims them, but this is incidental, not guaranteed. The proposed stable-handle design removes this class of stale-index bug outright. Recommend the finding call out that the redirector is both a leak and a latent out-of-bounds source.
